mcqs.question: Why can someone who has solved 200 problems untimed and alone still freeze in a real, timed, watched interview?
options: 200 problems is simply not enough volume regardless of practice mode
Untimed practice is inherently worthless and should never be used at any stage
Untimed solo practice removes the clock, the live observer, and the social cost of looking stuck — pressures that are specific to the live format and were never actually practiced
Solving problems alone always makes someone worse at solving them, regardless of format
mcqs.explanation: The gap is about which specific pressures were rehearsed, not raw volume — untimed solo practice never exposes someone to a visible clock, a live evaluator, or the social cost of stalling, so those specific muscles stay unpracticed regardless of how many problems were solved. Untimed practice has real value for learning new patterns; it just isn't sufficient alone, and more volume in the same mode doesn't fix the mismatch.

mcqs.question: Why do candidates self-administering a mock interview tend to skip the clarifying-questions and approach-stating phases first?
options: Because they feel like overhead when practicing alone, which is exactly why a realistic mock needs a partner or a strict script rather than just a stopwatch on a real problem
Because those phases are officially optional and don't need to be practiced
Because those phases only matter in phone screens, not full onsite rounds
Because clarifying questions are only useful for ambiguous problems, which are rare in practice sets
mcqs.explanation: Without a partner enforcing the round's real structure, the phases that feel like overhead when alone are the first to get skipped — which is precisely why a mock needs external structure, not just a timer on a normal practice problem. These phases matter in any round format, aren't officially skippable, and apply broadly, not just to obviously ambiguous prompts.

mcqs.question: What does reviewing a recording of a mock surface that live, in-the-moment feedback often misses?
options: Whether the final answer to the problem was correct

Pacing and pattern issues — dead silence before speaking, filler-word frequency, and whether stated complexity actually matches the code written — that are easier to notice looking back than to track while it's happening
Nothing new — a recording only repeats what a live observer would already have noted
Only the correctness of the code, not any communication issue
mcqs.explanation: A recording lets you notice pacing and pattern issues — silence, filler words, complexity mismatches — that are hard to track live while you're also focused on the problem itself, which is exactly its distinct value over live feedback. Final correctness is not the focus of this review, and a recording does surface things a live observer commonly misses.

mcqs.question: Why is a log of missed problems over several weeks more useful than reacting to any single missed problem?
options: Logging is mainly useful for showing an interviewer your practice history
A single missed problem always means the entire topic area needs to be restudied from scratch
Tracking is unnecessary if you simply solve more problems in general

A single miss is just one data point, while a log across weeks reveals whether there's a real recurring pattern — a specific technique, a timing issue, a skipped habit — turning a vague feeling into a concrete, addressable gap
mcqs.explanation: One miss doesn't reveal a pattern, but a log spanning multiple weeks can show whether the same specific issue recurs, which turns "I keep failing DP" into something concrete enough to target directly. The log isn't meant for showing an interviewer anything, a single miss doesn't imply restudying an entire topic, and undirected extra volume doesn't substitute for identifying the actual pattern.

mcqs.question: Per the platform-vs-mock-vs-pairing comparison, why does a realistic plan use all three modes rather than relying on just one?
options: Because they are functionally identical and using all three is only for variety

Because solo platform practice, formal mocks, and pairing with a friend each serve a different specific purpose — pattern exposure, full-fidelity pressure rehearsal, and cheap frequent narration practice — and none alone covers what the others provide
Because formal mock interviews alone are always sufficient and the other two modes are optional add-ons
Because pairing with a friend always produces more honest feedback than a formal mock
mcqs.explanation: Each mode has a distinct strength the others lack — platform practice for exposure and learning, mocks for full-pressure rehearsal, friend pairing for frequent low-cost narration practice — so combining them covers gaps any single mode leaves. They aren't interchangeable, mocks alone aren't sufficient given their cost and infrequency, and friend feedback can actually be softer, not more honest, than a stranger's.

mcqs.question: What's the common mistake in a multi-week practice plan leading up to an onsite?
options: Spending most of the available weeks in the easiest, most comfortable mode (untimed, known-pattern practice) and only reaching cold, timed mocks in the final days, leaving too little repetition of the mode that actually resembles the real interview
Starting cold, timed mock interviews too early in the plan, before any pattern review
Tapering practice volume at all before the onsite date
Including more than one practice mode in the same week
mcqs.explanation: The common failure is over-weighting the comfortable early stage and compressing the realistic, cold-mock stage into the final days, which under-rehearses the mode that most resembles the actual interview. Starting cold mocks early isn't the described mistake, a modest taper right before the onsite is actually recommended, and mixing modes within a week is not itself the problem.
